en: Waited and took his turn,
While his bitter foes fell still.
The noble lion’s descendant
Turned the head of his gray kulan steed
And leveled Manas the lion’s ornamented spear,
Making it thunder as he thrust.
Sarybay was his opponent,
Who had wrought such calamity;
Pouring out his wrath, Seytek shouted
And invoked the sacred spirit
Of Manas, his royal forefather.
He broke through forest and mountain to clear a road
And set his hand to a mountain-sized deed;
His battle cry deafened the ears.
He invoked the spirits of his ancestors
And of the many heroes of former cities,
Calling upon their sacred power,
And Seytek leveled his spear.
Sarybay, son of the ogre,
Knew well his own great strength
And now smiled beneath his mustache:
“I shall snuff out his burning lamp
And send him from this world;
I shall beat the fierce spirit from him.
Now I shall settle his account,
Make the boy scream,
And cut short his fly-sized soul.
I shall wreak boundless ruin
And take as spoil Kulansur,
The steed no bullet can catch.
The brute has run mad;
I shall soak his body in blood
And lay him down to grease the earth.
When he comes near, I shall cut off his head
And crush his liver like sausage.
This swine seeking blood
Has come to me himself,” he said.
“The raging champion’s time
To be slain here
Has now arrived,” he said.
“This young fool doomed to death,
This rabid cur,
Has come here himself,” he said.
“I shall roast him like wheat;
From this cur of a champion
I shall tear out the great artery of his head.
This wounded conqueror of foes—
I shall kill him and cut off his head,
And pierce his eyes, bright as Venus.
I shall unleash a mighty battle;
This boy is insolent,
So I shall settle his great account.”
He readied himself, gripping his axe,
While the other leveled his spear.
In less time than it takes to speak,
Urging on gray Kulansur,
Seytek reached him.
At the swine who came to face him,
He aimed his grooved steel ornamented spear
And drove it squarely toward the jaw.
Heedless when it struck,
The accursed Sarybay regarded
The thrust Seytek had delivered
As less than a touch upon his hem.
He neither swayed nor flinched;
The wrathful swine did not stir.
He did not die from that single thrust,
Nor did he reckon Seytek’s blow
Worthy even of a cough.
Pouring out his wrath, unconcerned,
Not counting the warrior his equal,
He deemed the fierce battle and great peril
Less than a touch upon his hem.
So Sarybay stood there,
While the noble, impassioned warrior
Gathered all his strength into his body.
Sarybay grew furious;
His menace was terrible, his venom strong—
Such was the villain.
The cunning boar
Was thick-armed and highly skilled,
Perfect in guile and fierce in venom,
Powerfully built and supreme,
One who had leveled the whole world.
At the sight of him, abandon hope;
Such was the accursed man.
All the powers in the world,
Countless conflicts, countless quarrels,
Countless perils, countless dark nights—
To all such things he was accustomed.
Wrathful Sarybay,
The many-muscled swine,
Bit hard upon his tongue
As his blood-drinking nature seized him.
His eyes blazed like a lion’s;
He bit his lips through,
And the swine would not cease until he had grappled.
Facing him in combat,
“I shall axe off his head,” he said,
“And reach the root of all he is.”
He roared menacingly,
Churning the blue heavens;
His beard and mustache bristled strand by strand,
And he thundered like an onrushing flood.
Anyone who watched him closely
Despaired of his borrowed mortal life.
Breaking through hills to make a road,
He attacked Seytek.
His black-jawed leather club
Deafened the ears when it struck.
The hide of a full-grown ox
Had been stretched over its core;
The hides of six wethers
Had been packed and braided around it.
Its grip was glassy,
Its wrist-loop stout as a jar;
Embers seemed set in its palm,
And blue thunderbolts lay within it.
Sarybay was adroit;
Such was his supreme courage.
He swung the leather club in a sweeping arc,
Then spurred the thoroughbred Tookyzyl,
Driving his heels into its flanks.
He aligned and wheeled his spear,
Thundered menacingly,
And spared no effort.
Its shaft was mounted with silver,
Its edge was faced with steel—
A steel-headed battle-axe.
Gripping it firmly, he braced himself,
Drew in his frame and made ready.
Fire poured from his mouth,
And his courage showed in full;
God had smitten him with fury.
Blood streamed from his charging steed,
And blood flowed along the path of his charge.
Growling in rising passion,
He thundered words to himself,
Raging and lunging,
Writhing with violent force;
His brows and lashes flared apart,
And venom poured from his mouth.
Toward the dauntless son of the hero
He turned and braced himself,
Straining and glaring with courage.
A mountain-like surge came to a halt,
Like a horse tethered to a post.
At the swine’s thunderous approach,
The accursed veteran
Readied his fire pit.
The black earth, without overturning,
Held firm beneath the massive weight.
The boar was rich in strength;
The skillful enemy Sarybay
Opened his mouth like a wolf,
And fire scattered before him.
He assumed a form of savage courage
And stirred grievous strife.
The mountain-like Tookyzyl
Broke the ground beneath its hooves;
He made Tookyzyl bound,
Spurring it right and left,
And lashing from side to side.
Pouring out his wrath, he shouted,
Raising the battle cry, “Where is he?”
His violent fury burst forth,
And he appeared like a mountain of black rock.
Sarybay was indeed a warrior;
Such was his conduct in combat.
Vision dimmed amid the tumult;
The battle, if seen, was a roaring storm.
Young Seytek, brave gray-maned wolf,
As Sarybay faced him
And began the savage slaughter,
Before an arrow could arrive,
Measured the place he must strike.
As the man rode to thrust at the boy,
“I have met my enemy—
May God prosper what follows;
May my forefather Manas uphold me,” he said.
Against the menacing villain,
Who swept away all he encountered,
The boar, warrior Sarybay,
The descendant of the brave gray wolf
Turned Kulansur’s head.
The father’s son
Did not fluster or hurry;
A descendant of his line
Never retreated from a foe,
Never fled after yielding ground,
Never thought, “I shall die,”
And never surrendered his courage to another.
The black-gray wolf, the peerless lion,
With strength compounded like packed sand,
Fought there in battle.
He measured and thrust toward the jaw:
“Just beneath the breast,
Right through the lung,
That is the place of death.”
Sarybay now leveled his spear:
“Right at the point of the jaw,
Right through the heart,
That is the measured spot.”
“For the grunting boar,
This is the moment of death,”
He said, taking aim with measured care.
At the raging infidel,
The warrior who had destroyed nations,
The youth rode up and thrust.
Both spears struck together,
And when the two spears hit,
They burst and splintered to pieces;
Fragments as large as tents
Flew whirling into the sky.
Those who watched and saw them,
As the two stood face-to-face
And in turn drove their spears
At one another,
Despaired of their lives.
Their bullet-proof armor split,
And Kulansur and Tookyzyl
Sank hoof-deep into the ground.
As the heroes met,
Their valor was revealed.
When they struck spears with cries of “Manas!”
The earth split five feet deep;
They trampled the ground beneath them,
Urging Kulansur on.
He flung forth his fury,
While that monstrous warrior, the wretch,
Grew angry with Tookyzyl.
It turned its deer-like neck;
Kulansur would not stand still,
While Tookyzyl was a true thoroughbred
That sprang up from the earth.
When they came beneath the horses,
Would Sarybay, son of the ogre,
Refrain from fighting?
His cavernous mouth opened,
And burning embers from the bit
Scattered in volleys.
His savage courage showed,
And he burned in bitter grief.
The cause of his grief
Was that Sarybay
Had never paid anyone the slightest heed;
No mortal had dared face him,
And he had never deigned to notice a mortal.
No one had ever leveled a spear at him;
He had bowed his neck to no one in the world,
And no one had ever challenged him.
Against that rabid boar,
None remained to ready a lasso.
Khans had died fighting him;
Every khan who clashed with him had died.
Warriors proud of their strength had died;
